metric.code_efficiency_conciseness.method: Inspected reusable comparison-language Python micro-benchmark programs (mb00-mb11) and adversarial programs under the assigned readable paths. Measured source line counts, syntactic density, and idiomatic construct usage relative to logic expressed.
metric.code_efficiency_conciseness.normalization_rationale: Python expresses pinned algorithms with low incidental boilerplate (comprehensions, tuple returns, no mandatory type annotations) but mandated data containers and ban on library acceleration force explicit loops, adding lines versus unconstrained idiomatic Python. Score 78/100 reflects strong-but-not-maximal conciseness under frozen, comparable workload constraints.
observations: mb04.py (FP arithmetic): 72 lines total; core workload() function is about 20 lines expressing nested loop over M=4000, R=75000 with 4 accumulators and comprehension-based array initialization.
mb07.py (merge sort): 104 lines total; msort() core algorithm implemented in about 35 lines using ping-pong buffer swap idiom (src, dst = dst, src), concise and idiomatic.
List/array comprehensions collapse multi-line init loops into single expressions.

Dynamic typing reduces declaration tokens, but pinned array('d')/array('q') containers and ban on vectorized/library-accelerated computation force explicit index loops for hot paths, adding lines versus idiomatic high-level Python with numpy.
No numpy/vectorization observed or permitted per the frozen binding table, equalizing conciseness comparisons across languages.
Adversarial programs (ADV-01..ADV-26) are uniformly very short (93-440 bytes), minimal single-purpose snippets with no incidental boilerplate.

metric.readability.method: Assessed naming, structure, docstrings, and control-flow clarity of the same reusable Python micro-benchmark and adversarial source files.
metric.readability.normalization_rationale: High readability score (88/100) reflects consistent naming, explanatory docstrings, uniform structure, and low syntactic noise typical of Python, with a small deduction for manual loop-increment style adopted for cross-language comparability.
observations: Every micro-benchmark file begins with a clear module docstring naming the workload, citing the frozen spec section, and stating forbidden shortcuts, aiding comprehension of intent versus implementation.
Helper class Lehmer (Park-Miller LCG) is small, uses __slots__, and has self-documenting method names (next_int, next_unit) repeated consistently across files.
Control flow uses plain while/for loops with descriptive local variable names (lo, mid, hi, i, j, k in mb07; s1..s4 accumulators in mb04) mirroring textbook algorithm descriptions.
CLI harness (main()) is identical in structure across files, reducing cognitive load across the corpus.
Significant whitespace and lack of braces/semicolons keep visual noise low; comments annotate non-obvious pinned-requirement constraints at point of relevance.
Minor cost: manual loop-increment style instead of augmented assignment/enumerate in some hot loops, adopted for cross-language performance comparability rather than idiomatic Python.
